newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges peace in Cambodia, says backs Sihanouk.
newsitem.headline: China urges peace in Cambodia, says backs Sihanouk.

text.p: China on Thursday called for a peaceful solution to the crisis in Cambodia and pledged Beijing's support for the authority and dignity of the nation's monarch, King Norodom Sihanouk.

Treading cautiously among old allies and former foes in Cambodia's warring forces, Beijing promised not to become involved in the internal affairs of a nation it once saw as a Maoist ideological ally.

"All parties in Cambodia should cherish the current peaceful situation and resolve current problems to prevent a deterioration of the situation," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang told a news briefing.

"China will never become involved in Cambodia's affairs," Tang said when asked to comment on the bloody July 6 coup in which Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen toppled rival First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh from power.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen told visiting counterparts from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) that Beijing supported attempts to bolster peace by Sihanouk, who is in the Chinese capital for medical treatment.

"China respects the status and role of Cambodian King Sihanouk, and stands for safeguarding his authority and dignity, and upholding the current form of the Cambodian government," the official Xinhua news agency quoted Qian as saying.

"What has happened in Cambodia belongs to internal affairs," Qian told the ministers from Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, who had earlier met Sihanouk at his palatial Beijing residence for talks on how to ease Cambodia's crisis.

"We hope the various parties concerned follow the guideline of national reconciliation advocated by Sihanouk, restore tranquillity as soon as possible, and make concerted efforts for peace, stability and development in the country," Qian said.

China has a long history of involvement in Cambodian politics and Beijing was the main military backer of the tripartite guerrilla movement spearheaded by the Maoist Khmer Rouge against Hun Sen's Vietnam-backed government in the 1980s.

China was a major supporter of the Khmer Rouge before and during their 1975-79 rule, when more than one million Cambodians are thought to have been killed, worked to death or fallen prey to disease because of a lack of medical care.
Beijing then saw the Khmer Rouge as adherents of a Maoist ideology of peasant revolution and thus natural allies against the rival brand of communism espoused by the Soviet Union.

China ended support to the rebels on the signing of the 1991 Cambodian peace pact, which it helped to broker as a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council. Chinese soldiers later served in the U.N. peacekeeping force in Cambodia.
Beijing's ties with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party have improved since the CPP joined a coalition government with two non-communist factions after the U.N.-sponsored 1993 elections.
Analysts said China had been cautious to avoid antagonising either Hun Sen or other factions following the most recent fighting in Cambodia.
